'''Harry Hindmarsh Atkinson''' (5 August 1929 – 30 December 2018) was a British physicist and science administrator.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr Harry Atkinson, 1929-2018 |url=https://www.esa.int/About_Us/ESA_history/Dr_Harry_Atkinson_1929-2018 |access-date=2024-03-30 |website=www.esa.int |language=en}}</ref> He served as chair of the [[European Space Agency]] Council between 1984 and 1987.

==Early life, family, and education==
Born in [[Wellington]], New Zealand, on 5 August 1929, Atkinson was the son of Constance Hindmarsh Atkinson (née Shields) and Harry Temple Atkinson, who served as head of the New Zealand Patent Office.<ref name="Stuff obituary">{{cite news |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/science/110294964/leading-kiwi-scientist-had-his-own-asteroid |title=Leading Kiwi scientist had his own asteroid |first=Duncan |last=Steel |date=7 February 2019 |work=Stuff.co.nz |access-date=16 May 2021}}</ref> His paternal grandfather was [[Harry Atkinson]], who had been prime minister of New Zealand on four occasions between 1876 and 1891.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/> The family moved to [[Nelson, New Zealand|Nelson]] when Atkinson was 12 years old, and he was educated at [[Nelson College]] from 1942 to 1947.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/><ref>{{cite book |chapter=Full school list of Nelson College, 1856–2005 |title=Nelson College Old Boys' Register, 1856–2006 |year=2006 |edition=6th |type=CD-ROM}}</ref>

Atkinson was influenced to study science by [[Thomas Easterfield]], and graduated from [[University of Canterbury|Canterbury University College]] with a [[Master of Science]] with first-class honours in physics in 1953.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://shadowsoftime.co.nz/university1.html |title=NZ university graduates 1870–1961: A |website=Shadows of Time |access-date=18 May 2021}}</ref> He then began doctoral studies at [[Cornell University]] in the United States in 1954, but moved to the [[University of Cambridge]] and the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] (AERE) under [[Neville Mott]] 18 months later, completing his [[PhD]] in 1959.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Atkinson, Harry |url=https://archives.eui.eu/en/isaar/136 |access-date=2024-03-30 |website=archives.eui.eu}}</ref> The title of his thesis was ''Small angle scattering of X-rays and neutrons from metals''.<ref>{{cite thesis |url=https://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/permalink/f/t9gok8/44CAM_ALMA21432613750003606 |title=Small angle scattering of X-rays and neutrons from metals |type=PhD |year=1959 |publisher=University of Cambridge |first=Harry Hindmarsh |last=Atkinson |access-date=18 May 2021}}</ref>

In 1958, Atkinson married Anne Barrett in [[Cambridge]], and the couple went on to have three children.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/>

==Scientific career==
After completing his doctorate, Atkinson remained at AERE at Harwell for several years, before moving to the nearby [[Rutherford Laboratory]] where he headed the general physics group for seven years. From 1968 to 1972, he was seconded to the office of the [[Government Chief Scientific Adviser (United Kingdom)|chief scientific advisor]] in the [[Cabinet Office]] in London, where he provided advice on a wide range of topics. Atkinson was appointed head of the [[Science Research Council]] astronomy and space division in 1972; his tenure saw Britain expand its research activity in astronomy, with new optical telescopes in Hawaii and the Canary Islands, and improvements to existing radio telescopes in England. When the European Space Agency (ESA) was formed in 1975, Atkinson became the British delegate to the ESA Council, and served as its vice chairman from 1981 to 1984 and chairman from 1984 to 1987. He also had operational oversight of several European nuclear physics research institutes during the 1980s.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/>

==Later life and death==
Although semi-retiring in 1990, Atkinson continued as chief scientist of the British insurance industry's Loss Prevention Council. In 2000, he chaired a task force investigating [[near-Earth object]]s, and in 2006 he was honoured when an asteroid orbiting the Sun between Mars and Jupiter was named [[Harryatkinson|5972 Harryatkinson]] by the [[International Astronomical Union]].<ref name="Stuff obituary"/>

In his later years, Atkinson suffered from dementia, and he died in [[Oxfordshire]] on 30 December 2018.<ref name="Stuff obituary"/>
